en: The feast fell quiet
Ak Kenen made camp
He took a spear because of the maiden
Moon-rider with winged sight
The lion’s favored one
The finest of the white-capped people
Bearing the people’s burden
A mountain hero from every side
His forty elder brothers were khans
Many different eyes beheld it
The formidable ones became united
He became a white-lion hero
He served the people
If he is the hero they described
We shall wind his turban
Thousands upon thousands stand here
If the hero’s gift is true
Without moving, we shall light the fire
Your march is like white wheat
Your advance is like a young antelope
Your true heart, steadfast Kozoy
All of us stirred
If he has many equals
Let that spoken word remain
No soul remained standing upon the earth
That was the time the khan was born
We shall set to digging and striving
Spilling blood unknown to the people
Many words came from one heart
Thus, my lady, he said
Now I have spoken, gentle Kanysh
Much land, dear Kanysh
Wisdom rests in the heart, Kanysh
You do not know the hero who is needed
Let his word become counsel to the hero
Your kinsman who stood as an equal
You are dear to them all, Kongdoy
Where is the day the current will flee
On such a day his people cry out
If I tell my people a thousand times
Giving a pledge from a pure heart
Without retreating or breaking his word
A word inherited from his ancestor
The ancestral spirit caused his name to be spoken
Your thousands came and formed ranks
Some went with greetings
Both a flower and a hero
The dear hero who knew the host
He himself gave blessing to Kozoy
His lineage produced a lion
What word was there
You yourself are the hero, Kenen
It was there in the stirrup
That remains from Manas
That red-faced one is the hero
He was strong as a stallion
He said this was his purpose
That white lion is the hero
An enemy road unknown to the people
The people’s arrival became a claim
Taking property to Kyz Manas
The hardship settled in the heart
The broken word was shattered
Ten more youths marched
When he came to his own words
If his father too was a hero
He ruled the people and founded a nation
One pale stallion for the Kazakh
If the hero’s breadth is vast
Calling them a thousand Kalmyks
The maiden was given to China
Friendship remained with me
The city was the pledge of the road
If he is a soul who knows no counsel
We shall address hero Kozoy
The people gathered and shouted the battle cry
The maidens wept as they sent him off
If I take his saddlebag, would that be wrong?
So the brave man thought.
Laying hands on it, people would say thus,
The chest remained unmoved,
His bag would remain over there.
The people did not throw the saddlebag down,
There was no one who would not yield to the dark deed,
Inside what he had awakened,
What is mine exists, but none will come,
Many took up spears,
His sieve and chest,
Mount the wind-swift steed,
Let him not pick it up from the ground,
As the holy old man had said,
The multitude overwhelmed by the enemy,
The host marched against the foe without turning back,
Take up your spear like that,
A fierce conflict arose on the opposing side,
Thinking it might fold its wings,
The host was left brimming with sorrow,
The people's spoken judgment—take it,
Is not the heart its seal—take it,
Reeling, reach for the horse,
Reach for the unwearied steed,
If it does not strike true, the brave man falls—take it,
With shield and battle-axe,
Draw your sword and wreak havoc,
The people, clutching the saddlebag, were in turmoil,
Where is the enemy, where is the friend,
The hero whose gaze beguiled—take him,
If I touch his property I would be a sinner—where is the foe?
Stand valuing his bravery—take it,
The people routed the enemy.
Then, at that moment, Aikanim,
The mountain beyond Kök was difficult,
Mount the trapped thoroughbred horse,
It turned out your lone devil,
In this numbered mortal world,
Riding on like a nightingale,
After the blood and the beginning,
The black belt appeared like a mountain,
The fleshy grave took the people,
The brave man took up his sword,
The fierce gray wolf took them all,
He struck without yielding,
The fox-mustached elder,
Strike with the black-tempered sword,
The tribes gathered into a host,
His voice grew sharper than steel,
The sandgrouse would rise at dawn,
Now he drove the army onward,
That place was the land of birches,
Seize hold of the lone greyhound,
One who never recoiled from death,
Whose voice carried across the world,
Who had the awesome presence of a dragon,
The striding racehorse
Almambet was urging onward,
Shouting, he drove it along the road.
On this side of him,
The most skillful of spearmen,
The finest among the countless Kyrgyz,
The foremost of brave men,
The champion of the forty companions,
This one too was born a lion,
Chubak, son of Akbalta.
With a piercing cry and a resounding battle shout,
No man's strength could match him in combat,
Even a lion's teeth could not pierce him,
Clad in a blue rapis coat,
Mounted on a blue-roan horse,
Huge as a mountain spur,
As though he would devour any enemy he saw.
Conspicuous beneath the battle standard,
Fire poured from his mouth,
When he shouted and leveled his spear,
He appeared like an army of forty thousand.
“It is my sister-in-law's horse,” he said,
“Her plea has reached me,” he said,
Dear valiant Chubak,
Urged it onward with exceptional force,
And he too raised the battle cry.
If you look farther ahead,
The edge of black steel,
Who found his way in darkness,
Who found the right words in an emergency,
Syrgak, lion-hearted Manas's man,
Who never stopped to rest on his elbow,
Who never slept even a wink,
Light on a horse and fit for a colt,
Always vigilant on the road,
The sleepless hero Syrgak,
Whose prowess could reach across the world,
Manas and this Syrgak
Were the sons of two brothers.
A keen-sighted, discerning hero,
Whenever a clamorous enemy came,
He drenched them in red blood,
Clad in deep-blue armor,
He rejoiced upon seeing a great host,
“Her plea has reached me,” he said,
“This is my sister-in-law's horse,” he said,
His bellow seemed to split heads,
His shout seemed to split stones,
Hero Syrgak, the young tiger,
The great lead-rope tied in a heavy knot,
He grasped with coils wound around his hand,
Towing Taitoru along,
Spurring from right and left,
He leaned forward and galloped,
His hem and sleeves fluttering,
He shouted and urged the horse onward.
Looking behind him,
With a face like polished wheat,
With eyes like twilight mist,
The black-mottled leopard,
Straining at his flank,
The short-maned blue lion,
Rode alongside, poised for action,
Your magnanimous hero of surpassing fortune,
For whom the wide world had become constricted.
Do not let it waver.
Without snapping at the weaker side.
Seemed to tremble.
Our people are poor and hard pressed.
Such a person must not be struck.
Without contending, he turned aside.
Many were bewildered, unable to find a way.
Many backed away from what had been said.
Trusting themselves to fate,
Many turned their steeds around.
With splendid swords at their waists,
They swarmed in fury.
Many stood obstinately.
Many people said, Let it be.
What times, what a day
Would come, and what a night?
Their full-grown strength overflowing,
Standing apart from the people,
Came before the valiant man,
Joining forces and making peace,
After a day, they pledged their word.
Heard that he too had a son.
Kenen, then three years old,
The hero's offspring, the girl,
You have a force ready to scatter at a movement.
Beside the hero Bolot,
There was a discerning judge of words.
All the weapons and equipment were there.
They had the wise Bolot as their khan.
All their abundant riches were there.
To Bolot upon the hill,
Displaying their precious finery,
Showing their white beards,
Riding horses that reared and plunged,
The lion-like warrior went on foot.
The resourceful hero Bolot,
The two imposing rulers,
Had come down the next morning.
Beside the hero Bolot,
Forty eminent, matchless champions,
Bent their knees,
Dismounted and hurried forward.
The warriors stood supporting one another.
They pressed toward the blue pavilion.
Showing their fierce mettle,
The young man's purpose was swift action.
Most were knowledgeable and keen-eyed.
The people were sending off the khan's daughter.
Are you some different kind of diviner?
Skilled in words and deeds,
A hero with a thousand troops,
Saying, The khan has come as marriage kin,
Join together to face the enemy,
Make your camp upon one hill.
If a formidable enemy appears,
Be united in purpose.
Is the advice spoken here bad?
Are the khans joined by marriage well?
